chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, prescriptions and math

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The job, the certifications and your state's rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare the PTCE and ExCPT exams and find your state's technician rules.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official PTCB, NHA and state board of pharmacy pages, you will compare the two national technician exams and write a study and test plan that meets your state's rules, with every requirement checked on an official page.
Pharmacy technicians take in prescriptions, type them into the computer, count and label medicine, manage stock, run the register and help customers. A pharmacist checks the work and answers every medicine question.
There are two national certifications, and both give the title Certified Pharmacy Technician (CPhT). PTCB, the Pharmacy Technician Certification Board, gives it to people who pass the PTCE. Its eligibility includes a PTCB-recognized training program or enough work experience. NHA, the National Healthcareer Association, gives it to people who pass the ExCPT, with a training program or supervised work experience.
Your state board of pharmacy decides what technicians may do and whether you must register or be licensed before you work. Rules differ a lot between states. The National Association of Boards of Pharmacy (NABP) lists every state board.
Fees, eligibility and exam rules change, and both certifications ask you to report criminal or board actions. Read the official pages before you pay. This course prepares you; it does not certify or register you.
Step by step:
- Open PTCB's CPhT page and NHA's pharmacy technician page.
- Write down for each: the exam name, how you qualify and how often you renew.
- Find your state board of pharmacy on the NABP list.
- Write what your state requires before you can work as a technician.
- Pick your exam and a target month.
Words to know:
- Pharmacy technician: a trained worker who helps the pharmacist prepare and give out medicine.
- Pharmacist: the licensed professional who checks prescriptions and advises patients about medicine.
- CPhT: Certified Pharmacy Technician, the title given by PTCB or NHA after their exams.
- State board of pharmacy: the state agency that licenses pharmacists and sets rules for technicians.
Official sources:
- PTCB: Certified Pharmacy Technician (CPhT)
- NHA: Certified Pharmacy Technician (ExCPT)
- NABP: State boards of pharmacy
Try it now: Make a two-column table: PTCE and ExCPT. Fill in who gives it, how you qualify and how often you renew, from the official pages. Under it, write what your state board of pharmacy requires before you can work as a technician, and the web address where you found it.
You can now say what technicians do, name the two national exams and who gives them, and find your state's technician rules.

options: PTCB, the Pharmacy Technician Certification Board
check.why: PTCB gives the PTCE; passing it earns PTCB's CPhT.

check.q: Who decides whether you must register before working as a technician?
check.why: Each state board of pharmacy sets technician registration and practice rules.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading a prescription
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Name the parts of a practice prescription and rewrite its directions in plain words.
This lesson builds toward: Given a made-up prescription, you will name its parts and rewrite the directions in plain words, getting at least 4 of 5 practice prescriptions fully right.
A prescription has set parts: the patient's name and date of birth, the drug name, the strength (for example 10 mg), the dosage form (tablet, capsule, liquid), the directions (called the sig), the quantity, the number of refills, the date, and the prescriber's name and signature.
Directions often use Latin abbreviations. Common ones: po (by mouth), bid (twice a day), tid (three times a day), qid (four times a day), prn (as needed), hs (at bedtime). The label must be in plain words, so "1 tab po bid" becomes "Take 1 tablet by mouth twice a day."
Some abbreviations cause errors, so safety groups say not to use them. For example, "QD" (daily) has been mistaken for "QID" (four times a day), and "U" for units has been read as a zero. Also watch decimals: write 0.5 mg (with a leading zero), never .5 mg, and never 5.0 mg (a trailing zero can be read as 50).
If anything is unclear, missing or looks wrong, do not guess. Flag it for the pharmacist.
Step by step:
- Check the patient's name and date of birth.
- Find the drug name, strength and dosage form.
- Read the sig and rewrite it in plain words.
- Check the quantity, refills, date and prescriber.
- Flag anything unclear or missing for the pharmacist.
Words to know:
- Sig: the directions on a prescription that tell the patient how to take the medicine.
- Strength: how much drug is in each unit, for example 10 mg in one tablet.
- Dosage form: the kind of medicine: tablet, capsule, liquid, cream and so on.
- Refill: a permitted repeat of the same prescription.
- Prescriber: the licensed person who wrote the prescription, such as a doctor or nurse practitioner.
Try it now: Practice only, made-up drugs. Rewrite each sig in plain words: (1) "Drug X 1 tab po bid" (2) "Drug Y 2 caps po hs" (3) "Drug Z 1 tab po q6h prn". Answers: (1) Take 1 tablet by mouth twice a day. (2) Take 2 capsules by mouth at bedtime. (3) Take 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed. Then list the parts that are missing from this note: "Drug X 10 mg, #30, Dr. Lee".
You can now name the parts of a prescription, read common sig abbreviations, spot error-prone writing and flag unclear orders.

check.q: In practice, what does "1 tab po tid" mean?
options: Take 1 tablet by mouth three times a day
check.why: po means by mouth and tid means three times a day.

check.q: A practice prescription has no directions (sig). What do you do?
options: Ask the customer how they take it
check.why: A missing or unclear part is never guessed; the pharmacist handles it with the prescriber.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Practice pharmacy math
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Solve practice-only problems for conversions, quantity and days' supply.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice-only problems with made-up numbers and a basic calculator, you will solve pharmacy math problems for unit conversions, quantity and days' supply, getting at least 8 of 10 right with the work shown.
Practice only: these are made-up numbers for exam practice, never directions for a real patient. In real work the pharmacist checks every calculation.
Conversions to know: 1 gram (g) = 1,000 milligrams (mg). 1 liter (L) = 1,000 milliliters (mL). 1 kilogram (kg) is about 2.2 pounds (lb). 1 teaspoon (tsp) = 5 mL and 1 tablespoon (tbsp) = 15 mL. 1 fluid ounce is about 30 mL.
Days' supply tells how long the medicine will last: days' supply = quantity ÷ amount used per day. Practice: Drug X, 1 tablet twice a day, 60 tablets. Used per day = 2. 60 ÷ 2 = 30 days. Quantity works the other way: quantity = amount per day × days. Practice: Drug Y, 1 capsule three times a day for 10 days = 3 × 10 = 30 capsules.
Always write the units, set up the problem before you press the calculator, and check if the answer makes sense. A 30-day supply of 6,000 tablets does not.
Step by step:
- Write what you know, with units.
- Write what you need to find.
- Convert to the same units if needed.
- Set up the problem, then calculate.
- Ask: does the answer make sense?
Words to know:
- mg: milligram: one thousandth of a gram.
- mL: milliliter: one thousandth of a liter.
- Days' supply: how many days a prescription will last if taken as directed.
- Conversion: changing a number from one unit to another, like grams to milligrams.
Try it now: Practice only, made-up numbers. Solve and show your work: (1) 2.5 g = ? mg (2) 3 tsp = ? mL (3) 132 lb = ? kg (4) Drug X, 1 tablet 3 times a day, 90 tablets: days' supply? (5) Drug Y, 2 capsules twice a day for 14 days: quantity? Answers: 2,500 mg; 15 mL; 60 kg; 30 days; 56 capsules.
You can now convert common units and work out days' supply and quantity on practice problems, showing your work.

check.q: Practice only: how many milligrams are in 0.5 grams?
Practice only: Drug X, 1 tablet twice a day, 28 tablets. What is the days' supply?
check.why: Days' supply = 28 tablets ÷ 2 per day = 14 days.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Safety checks: the right drug for the right patient
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a practice order against the prescription and flag any mismatch.
This lesson builds toward: Given a filled practice order and its stock bottle, you will check the patient, drug, strength and NDC against the prescription and flag any mismatch, catching every planted mismatch.
Most errors come from small slips: the wrong patient, a drug with a similar name, the wrong strength, or the wrong bottle from the shelf. Technicians help catch them before the pharmacist's final check.
Use two patient identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, every time you take in or hand out a prescription. Two people can have the same name.
Every drug package has a National Drug Code (NDC), the FDA's three-part number that identifies the maker, the product and the package. Matching the NDC on the stock bottle to the one in the computer (often by scanning the barcode) confirms you picked the right drug, strength and package. The FDA plans to change NDCs to one 12-digit format in the future, so learn the idea, not one length.
Watch for look-alike and sound-alike drug names. Read the full name, the strength and the form on the bottle, not just the first letters. If anything does not match, stop and tell the pharmacist.
Step by step:
- Confirm two patient identifiers: name and date of birth.
- Compare the drug name on the bottle with the prescription, letter by letter.
- Compare the strength and the dosage form.
- Scan or compare the NDC on the stock bottle.
- Stop and flag any mismatch for the pharmacist.
Words to know:
- NDC: National Drug Code: the FDA's three-part number for a drug's maker, product and package.
- Patient identifiers: details such as full name and date of birth used to make sure you have the right person.
- Look-alike, sound-alike drugs: drugs with names that look or sound similar and are easy to mix up.
- Stock bottle: the large container the pharmacy counts medicine from.
Official sources:
- FDA: National Drug Code Directory
Try it now: Practice only. Write three made-up practice orders on paper, each with a patient name, date of birth, drug, strength and NDC. Have a friend copy them as "stock bottle labels" and secretly change one detail in two of them. Compare each pair the way you learned and circle every mismatch.
You can now check a practice order against the prescription with two patient identifiers and the NDC, and flag every mismatch.

check.q: Which pair is two patient identifiers?
options: Full name and date of birth
check.why: Full name and date of birth are commonly used together to confirm the right patient.

check.q: The NDC on the stock bottle does not match the computer. What do you do?
options: Fill it anyway; the name is close
check.why: An NDC mismatch can mean the wrong drug, strength or package, so you stop and flag it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Your role, the pharmacist's role and controlled substances
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort practice tasks into technician work or pharmacist work.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice pharmacy situations, you will sort each task into technician work or pharmacist work and follow the extra rules for controlled substances, sending every clinical question to the pharmacist.
Technicians do technical work: take in and enter prescriptions, count, label, manage stock, process insurance and help at the register. Pharmacists do the clinical work: the final check, counseling about how to take a medicine, side effects, drug interactions and any "Is this safe for me?" question. Your state sets the exact line, so learn your state's rules.
A simple rule: if a customer asks about their health or their medicine, the answer is "Let me get the pharmacist for you." Never give your own advice, even if you think you know.
Controlled substances are drugs the federal Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) places in Schedules I to V, based on their accepted medical use and their risk of misuse and dependence. Schedule I drugs have no accepted medical use in the US; Schedule II drugs have a high risk of misuse; risk gets lower toward Schedule V. They have extra rules for storage, counting, records and refills, and states can add more.
For exams, know the five schedules, that the pharmacy keeps careful records of every controlled drug, and that any missing count is reported to the pharmacist right away.
Step by step:
- Ask: is this a technical task or a health question?
- Technical: do it carefully, following store policy and state rules.
- Health or medicine question: get the pharmacist.
- Controlled substance: follow the extra rules for counts, records and storage.
- Anything missing or odd: tell the pharmacist right away.
Words to know:
- Counseling: when the pharmacist explains to a patient how to take a medicine and what to watch for.
- Controlled substance: a drug the law controls more closely because it can be misused or cause dependence.
- DEA: the Drug Enforcement Administration, the federal agency that enforces controlled substance laws.
- Schedule: one of five groups (I to V) that controlled substances are placed in.
Official sources:
- DEA: Drug scheduling
- NABP: State boards of pharmacy (technician rules)
Try it now: Practice only. Sort these into Technician or Pharmacist: (1) counting tablets for a filled order, (2) a customer asks if she can take her new medicine with her allergy pills, (3) restocking a delivery, (4) a customer asks what side effects to expect, (5) entering a new prescription. Answers: 1, 3 and 5 Technician; 2 and 4 Pharmacist. Then write the exact words you will say to send a question to the pharmacist.
You can now tell technician work from pharmacist work, send every health question to the pharmacist, and name the five controlled substance schedules.

check.q: A customer asks if his new medicine is safe with alcohol. What do you say?
options: "Let me get the pharmacist for you."
check.why: Questions about safety and interactions are clinical; only the pharmacist answers them.

check.q: Which federal agency places drugs in Schedules I to V?
check.why: The DEA enforces the controlled substance schedules.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Privacy at the counter, and your study plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Share patient information only with people who need it, and only what they need.
This lesson builds toward: At the pharmacy counter or on the phone, you will share patient information only with people who need it, and only the minimum they need, in every practice situation, following HIPAA.
A pharmacy holds private health information: names, birth dates, medicines, insurance. HIPAA, the federal health privacy law, protects it. Its "minimum necessary" idea means you use and share only what is needed for the task.
At the counter: speak quietly, do not read drug names out loud for the line to hear, and confirm two identifiers before handing over a bag. On the phone: confirm who is calling before you share anything, and follow store policy on who may pick up for someone else.
Never post about customers, never look up a neighbor's or a famous person's record out of curiosity, and keep screens and paperwork out of sight. Report privacy mistakes to the pharmacist or privacy officer right away.
Now build your final task: your study and test plan and practice workbook.
Step by step:
- Ask: does this person need this information for their job or care?
- Share only the minimum they need.
- Confirm two identifiers before handing out medicine.
- Speak quietly and keep screens and papers hidden.
- Report privacy mistakes right away.
Words to know:
- HIPAA: the federal law that protects the privacy and security of health information.
- PHI: protected health information: health information that can identify a person.
- Minimum necessary: using or sharing only the information needed for the task.
Official sources:
- HHS: HIPAA for professionals (Privacy Rule)
- PTCB: Certified Pharmacy Technician (CPhT)
Try it now: Final task. Write your study and test plan: the exam (PTCE or ExCPT), what your state board requires, and weekly study dates up to a target test date. Attach your practice workbook: 5 made-up prescriptions you read and checked, 10 practice math problems with work shown, and 5 customer questions you would send to the pharmacist. Use no real patient information.
You can now protect patient privacy at the counter and on the phone, and follow your own written plan toward a pharmacy technician exam.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Study and test plan No exam named, or the state's rules are missing or guessed. Names the exam and who gives it, the state board's requirement with its web address, and weekly dates to a test date. Also names a training program and how the learner will meet the exam's eligibility. Prescriptions read Fewer than 4 of 5 prescriptions read correctly, or a missing part was not flagged. At least 4 of 5 practice prescriptions have all parts named and directions in plain words. All 5 are right, and every error-prone abbreviation is spotted. Practice math Fewer than 8 of 10 right, or no work shown. At least 8 of 10 practice problems right, with units and work shown. 10 of 10 right, with a sense check written for each answer. Safety checks A planted mismatch was missed. Every planted mismatch in name, strength or NDC was circled. Explains how each mismatch could have harmed a patient. Pharmacist questions Gives own advice on a health question. Lists 5 customer questions that go to the pharmacist and the words to hand them over. Also explains the extra rules for controlled substances. Privacy Uses real patient information anywhere in the workbook. Uses only made-up information. Lists three counter or phone habits that protect privacy. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A caller says he is a customer's neighbor and asks what medicine she picked up. What do you do?
options: Tell him; he is just being kind
Share nothing and follow store policy
Tell him only the first medicine
check.why: HIPAA protects her information; a neighbor has no right to it.

check.q: What helps protect privacy at the counter?
options: Speaking quietly and confirming two identifiers
Leaving bags open on the counter
Showing the screen to the line
check.why: Quiet voices and identity checks keep health information private.
